title: Exact Realization of Deep ReLU Computation in a Microscopic Statistical-Mechanical System
abstract: Understanding the physical origin of the piecewise-linear computation in deep rectified linear unit (ReLU) networks remains a fundamental challenge. Here we establish an exact statistical-mechanical realization of arbitrary ReLU networks. Starting from a microscopic configuration space and its state multiplicities, we construct a partition function without prescribing a neural-network activation function. The resulting system admits equivalent descriptions in terms of cascaded quantum operations with post selection, or fermionic transport model. We rigorously prove that in $β\to+\infty$ limit, the thermodynamic observables of this system exactly reproduce the hidden states, outputs, and loss function of an arbitrary deep ReLU network. Crucially, we demonstrate that the piecewise-linear behavior of the ReLU network emerges from a first-order phase transition in the microscopic system, where the discontinuities precisely coincide with the boundaries of linear regions of ReLU network. This work establishes an exact physical foundation for deep neural computation and provides a novel statistical-mechanical perspective on neural architecture design.
summary: This work provides an exact physical foundation for deep ReLU network computation by mapping it onto a microscopic statistical-mechanical system. The authors show that the network's piecewise-linear behavior arises precisely from a first-order phase transition within the system's thermodynamics. This establishes a deep link between condensed matter physics concepts and modern machine learning theory.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental challenge of finding a physical origin for the piecewise-linear computation characteristic of deep ReLU networks.
main_result: It establishes an exact statistical-mechanical realization of arbitrary deep ReLU networks, showing that their behavior emerges from a first-order phase transition in the underlying microscopic system.
method: The authors use statistical mechanics, analyzing a partition function derived from a microscopic configuration space, and taking the zero-temperature limit ($ eta 	o +\infty$).
model_or_system: The model is a microscopic statistical-mechanical system, equivalently described by cascaded quantum operations with post-selection or a fermionic transport model.
key_observables: Population imbalance ($z(t)$), hidden states, outputs, and the loss function of the ReLU network.
important_parameters: The inverse temperature parameter $ eta$, which is taken to $+\infty$ (zero-temperature limit).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on the zero-temperature limit ($ eta 	o +\infty$) and the interpretation of the system dynamics via fermionic transport.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical realization of affine transformations using quantum circuits and fermionic transport models, and plot the derivative of the effective potential showing discontinuities coinciding with ReLU boundaries.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the physical system and its quantum/fermionic descriptions, then deriving the partition function using post-selection, and finally proving the correspondence by analyzing the ensemble average in the $ eta 	o +\infty$ limit.
why_interesting: The connection between phase transitions in statistical mechanics and the sharp, non-analytic behavior (piecewise linearity) of deep learning models provides a novel physical lens for understanding artificial intelligence.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Physical realization of an affine transformation and its fermionic transport interpretation. (a) A quantum circuit block implementing the affine map f W (t). After measurement, the control and target outcomes are recorded as σ(t) ∈{0, 1} and s(t), respectively. Shots with s(t) ∈{1, . . . , dt} are passed to the next block, whereas shots with s(t) > dt are discarded. (b) Representation as a fermionic transport model. The tth column contains dt effective sites, and each spin-1/2 fermion represents one shot. The fermion propagates from one column to the next, eg, from site st−1 in the t −1-th column to the st site in the next, where spin-up and spin-down states correspond to σ(t) = 0...

FIG. 2: Exact mapping and temperature-driven condensation. (a) Prediction of the trained ReLU network (red dashed line) versus the target ˆy = sin(πˆx) + 1 (black solid line). Inset: zoom-in showing the piecewise linearity. (b) Comparison of the training loss (black dashed line) and the ensemble loss (solid lines) across different β. (c) The rescaled output (QT τ=0 C(τ))g for various β, showing the transition from a disordered linear state (β = 0) to the exact ReLU output (β = 100). (d) Maximum probability max q(α) versus input ˆx, demonstrating the condensation to the eα.

FIG. 3: First-order phase transition underlying ReLU piecewise linearity. The derivative ⟨∂Π/∂x⟩as a function of input ˆx for various β. At low β, The derivative is continuous (β = 0, flat line). As β increases, discontinuities emerge (β = 100, red crosses). These discontinuities align exactly with the boundaries of the linear pieces in the ReLU network (see Fig. 1(a)), demonstrating that the piecewise linear behavior is a macroscopic manifestation of a first-order phase transition.
